description.en: The all fours quad stretch is a hip flexor and quad stretch performed from a hands and knees start. The lifter lifts one leg up and reaches back to grab the foot, pulling the heel toward the glute. It is a useful warm-up and recovery stretch.

en: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lift one foot up toward the ceiling.
Reach back with the same side hand and grab the lifted foot.
Gently pull the heel toward the glute to stretch the quad.
Hold the stretch with steady breath.
Release the foot and lower it back down.
Switch sides and repeat.
Strong quad stretch
Stretches the hip flexors
Useful warm-up move
No equipment needed
Builds hip mobility
Easy to do anywhere

description.en: The band seated wide grip row is performed seated on the floor with the elbows flared wide during the pull. The flared elbow angle biases the upper back, rhomboids, and rear delts over the lats. It is great for building upper back detail and improving posture.

en: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front of you.
Loop a resistance band around both feet.
Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing down.
Sit upright with a tall, straight back.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Pull the handles back toward your upper chest with elbows flared wide.
Lead with the elbows out to the sides at shoulder height.
Squeeze the upper back hard, then return slowly.
Builds upper back detail
Targets rhomboids and rear delts
Improves posture
Easy to set up at home
Joint-friendly variation
Strong upper back builder

description.en: The band standing straight arm pulldown anchors a resistance band overhead and pulls the band handles down to the hips with straight arms. The straight-arm setup eliminates biceps involvement and isolates the lats hard. It is a great home version of the cable straight arm pulldown.

en: Anchor a resistance band overhead.
Stand facing the anchor with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grab a handle in each hand with arms extended overhead.
Step back slightly to add tension.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Keep your arms straight throughout the entire movement.
Pull the handles down to your thighs by driving them down with the lats.
Squeeze the lats hard at the bottom, then return slowly.
Strict lat isolation
Eliminates biceps involvement
Easy to set up at home
No machine required
Builds back width
Strong lat finisher

description.en: The barbell deadlift from deficit is performed standing on a small platform or weight plates, raising your feet so the bar starts below your normal floor position. The extended range of motion forces a deeper hinge and more knee bend, building bottom-end strength right where most lifters are weakest.

en: Stand on a small platform or 25 to 45 pound weight plates, around 1 to 4 inches tall.
Set up over a loaded barbell with your feet hip-width apart.
Bend at the hips and knees to reach the bar with your hands just outside your legs.
Pull the slack out of the bar and engage your lats.
Brace your core hard. The deeper start position requires more bracing.
Drive through your feet to lift the bar off the floor.
Stand up tall with the bar, locking out hips and knees.
Lower the bar with control back to the platform.
Extended range of motion builds bottom-end strength
Forces deeper hinge and stronger leg drive
Develops explosive drive off the floor
Builds quad and glute strength at the start of the pull
Improves competition deadlift starting position
Tougher than standard deadlifts at the same weight

description.en: The barbell seated close grip concentration curl is a seated barbell curl variation with the elbows resting on the inner thighs in a concentration curl position. The close grip emphasizes the long head and inner bicep peak. The seated thigh-supported position eliminates body english and isolates the biceps.

en: Sit on the end of a flat bench with feet wide on the floor.
Hold a barbell with a close, underhand grip about shoulder-width or narrower.
Lean forward slightly and rest your elbows on the inner thighs.
Allow the bar to hang at full arm extension.
Brace your core and keep your back straight.
Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control to a full stretch.
Strict concentration curl pattern
Eliminates body english
Close grip emphasizes inner bicep
Builds bicep peak
Strong stretch at the bottom
Useful for bicep specialization

description.en: The barbell standing rocking leg calf raise combines a standing calf raise with a rocking motion onto the heels. With a barbell across the upper back, you press up onto the toes for a calf raise, then rock back onto the heels with toes lifted. The combination trains both the calves and the tibialis anterior.

en: Position a barbell across your upper back behind the neck.
Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Brace your core and stay tall through the torso.
Press up through the balls of your feet, lifting the heels.
Squeeze the calves at the top.
Lower back down through neutral.
Rock back onto your heels by lifting the toes off the floor.
Lower the toes back down. Continue rocking forward and back.
Trains calves and tibialis anterior
Combined calf and shin work
Builds ankle stability
Different stimulus than standard calf raise
Useful for lower leg balance
Heavy progressive loading

description.en: The barbell standing snatch grip shrug is performed with a very wide snatch grip on the bar. The wide grip activates more rhomboid and middle trap work than a standard shrug while also building strength and capacity in the snatch grip position. It is a strong accessory for Olympic lifters.

en: Stand with a barbell at hip level, gripping it with a snatch-width grip.
Use a grip width well outside the shoulders, near the rings on a standard barbell.
Stand tall with chest up and shoulders pulled back.
Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Hold the contraction at the top for one count.
Lower the bar back down slowly with control.
Avoid rolling your shoulders. Move them straight up and straight down.
Wide grip increases middle trap and rhomboid engagement
Builds strength in the snatch grip position
Strong carryover to Olympic lifting
Allows heavy progressive loading
Builds upper trap mass
Useful accessory for Olympic lifters

description.en: The cable kneeling single lat pulldown is a single-arm lat pulldown performed from a half-kneeling position. The half-kneeling stance and single-arm action force strict pulling form and isolate each lat individually. It is a strong choice for correcting lat imbalances and improving the mind-muscle connection.

en: Set a cable to the highest pulley with a single handle.
Kneel on one knee facing the cable.
Grip the handle with the same-side arm as the kneeling leg.
Extend the arm overhead toward the pulley.
Brace your core and stand tall through the torso.
Pull the handle down and toward your shoulder by bending the elbow.
Squeeze your lat hard at the bottom of the pull.
Slowly extend the arm overhead to the starting position. Switch sides.
Strict single-arm lat work
Corrects lat imbalances
Improves mind-muscle connection
Half-kneeling base eliminates body english
Constant cable tension
Builds lat width and detail

description.en: The cable low seated row with V bar is a classic seated cable row done with a V bar attachment. The narrow neutral grip targets the mid back and lats. The seated position keeps the form strict and builds upper back size.

en: Sit at a cable row station with feet on the platform.
Grip the V bar with both hands palms facing each other.
Sit tall with the back straight and chest up.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades.
Pull the V bar toward the lower ribs.
Drive the elbows back close to the sides.
Squeeze the lats hard at the back.
Extend the arms with control to the start.
Builds the lats
Trains the mid back
Strong neutral grip row
Builds back size
Useful classic move
Builds the biceps

description.en: The cable rope high-pulley overhead tricep extension is a tricep isolation exercise where you face away from a high cable pulley with a rope attachment, extending at the elbows to push the rope overhead. The rope allows you to split your hands at lockout for a stronger contraction and provides a deep stretch on the long head of the triceps.

en: Attach a rope handle to a high cable pulley. Grip both ends of the rope.
Face away from the cable machine. Step forward and lean slightly. The rope should be behind your head with elbows bent.
Stagger your stance for stability. Brace your core. Pin your upper arms in place.
Extend at the elbows to push the rope forward and overhead. As you reach lockout, split the rope ends apart.
Squeeze your triceps hard for one second at lockout.
Slowly let the rope travel back behind your head over two to three seconds. Feel the deep stretch.
Keep your upper arms still throughout — only the forearms move.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Rope allows extra range of motion and hand splitting at lockout
Deep stretch on the long head of the triceps
Constant cable tension throughout the range
Easier on the elbows than barbell overhead extensions
Excellent finisher for tricep workouts
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The cable standing cross over high reverse fly is a rear delt fly using two high cables in a crossover. The lifter grips a high cable in each hand crossing the arms in front, then pulls them wide and back. The constant tension hammers the rear delts.

en: Set both cables to a high position with single handles.
Stand in the center of a cable crossover.
Reach across the body to grip the opposite high cable in each hand.
Cross the arms at chest height.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Pull the arms wide and back uncrossing them.
Continue back until the arms are out to the sides at shoulder height.
Squeeze the rear delts hard. Return with control.
Strong rear delt builder
Constant cable tension
Trains the upper back
Builds rear delt size
Useful posture builder
Strong cable move

description.en: The cable twisting standing high row is similar to the twisting standing row but uses a high cable position, pulling downward and across the body with rotation. It targets the upper back, rear delts, and obliques through a diagonal pulling pattern.

en: Set a cable pulley to a high position. Attach a D-handle.
Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand, arm extended up toward the cable.
Torso rotated toward the cable to start.
Pull the handle down and across your body toward your opposite hip while rotating your torso.
Squeeze your upper back and obliques at the end position.
Return to start under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Diagonal pulling pattern targets upper back and obliques
Combines high row with rotation
Constant cable tension
Functional pulling pattern
Easy to load progressively
Builds shoulder and core together

description.en: The cable wide grip lat pulldown is a vertical pulling exercise performed at a high cable pulley with a wide bar attachment. The wide overhand grip shifts emphasis to the upper lats and teres major, making it the go-to exercise for building back width and that V-taper look. It is one of the most accessible lat builders for lifters who cannot yet do bodyweight pull-ups.

en: Attach a long lat pulldown bar to a high cable pulley. Adjust the thigh pad so it firmly secures your legs.
Reach up and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands wider than shoulder-width — roughly where the bar bends down at the ends.
Sit down with your thighs locked under the pad. Lean back slightly (about 10 to 15 degrees) and stick your chest out.
Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position.
Pull the bar down by driving your elbows down and out toward your hips. Lead with your elbows, not your hands.
Bring the bar to your upper chest, just below your collarbones. Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom.
Slowly let the bar travel back up under control until your arms are fully extended overhead. Feel the stretch in your lats.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Avoid using momentum or leaning back excessively.
Builds the upper lats and back width more than narrow-grip variations
Excellent regression for lifters who cannot yet do pull-ups
Easy to load progressively with small weight increments
Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion
Trains the lats through a long stretch and full contraction
Carries over to pull-up and chin-up strength

description.en: The crab walk is a full-body conditioning exercise where you support yourself in a reverse-tabletop position (face up, hands and feet on the floor) and walk forward, backward, or sideways. It builds tricep, glute, and core strength while challenging coordination and shoulder stability.

en: Sit on the floor with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat. Place your hands behind you on the floor with fingers pointing toward your feet.
Lift your hips off the floor so your torso is parallel to the ceiling. Form a reverse-tabletop position.
Begin walking forward by alternating opposite hand and foot.
Move your right hand and left foot forward, then your left hand and right foot.
Keep your hips lifted throughout. Do not let them drop.
Walk for the desired distance (10 to 30 feet) or time.
To return, walk backward in the same pattern.
Move slowly with control — this is harder than it looks.
Builds tricep and shoulder endurance
Strengthens the glutes and hamstrings
Trains core stability through dynamic movement
Improves coordination and body awareness
No equipment needed
Counteracts hunched-forward posture

description.en: The dumbbell bent-over reverse row performs a bent-over row with a supinated (underhand) grip. The underhand grip shifts emphasis to the biceps and lower lats, and allows the elbows to tuck close to the body during the pull.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding dumbbells with an underhand grip (palms forward).
Hinge at the hips to roughly 45 degrees. Back flat.
Let the dumbbells hang with arms extended.
Row both dumbbells toward your hips, driving your elbows back along your sides.
Squeeze your lats at the top.
Lower under control.
The underhand grip recruits the biceps and lower lats.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Underhand grip increases bicep involvement
Emphasizes the lower lats
Elbows naturally tuck for lat focus
Builds back thickness
Different stimulus from overhand rows
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The dumbbell forward leaning lunge is a forward lunge variation where you intentionally lean your torso forward as you descend. The forward lean shifts emphasis from the quads to the glutes and hamstrings, making it a strong glute-focused alternative to the standard upright lunge.

en: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Step forward with your right leg into a forward lunge.
As you lower, lean your torso forward over your front thigh.
Continue down until your back knee approaches the floor.
Keep your front foot flat and push your hips back slightly.
Drive through the front heel to step back to the starting position while standing back upright.
Repeat on the other leg, alternating sides.
Shifts emphasis from quads to glutes
Builds glute and hamstring strength
Improves hip mobility
Single-leg work corrects imbalances
Reduces stress on the knees compared to upright lunges
Strong carryover to athletic hip drive

description.en: The dumbbell lying one arm deltoid rear is a unilateral rear delt fly performed lying on the side on an incline bench. The lifter holds a dumbbell with the working arm and lifts it up and back. The lying position stabilizes the chest and isolates the rear delt.

en: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees.
Lie on your side on the bench with the lower side flat against the pad.
Hold a dumbbell in the top hand with arm hanging down.
Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blade.
Lift the dumbbell up and back in a wide arc.
Stop when the arm is parallel to the floor.
Squeeze the rear delt hard at the top.
Lower with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong rear delt isolation
Stabilizes the chest
Builds upper back thickness
Useful posture builder
Strong dumbbell move
Trains the rhomboids

description.en: The dumbbell one leg squat is a unilateral squat performed standing on one leg with the other extended in front, while holding dumbbells. The dumbbells provide a counterbalance that helps you stay upright and adds load to the working leg. It is a strong progression toward bodyweight pistol squats.

en: Stand on your right leg with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Lift your left leg out in front of you, keeping it extended.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Allow the dumbbells to act as a counterbalance.
Lower into a single-leg squat by bending your right knee.
Keep the non-working leg extended forward throughout.
Continue down until your thigh approaches parallel to the floor.
Drive up through your right heel to stand back to the starting position. Switch legs.
Builds single-leg strength
Dumbbells act as counterbalance
Stepping stone to bodyweight pistol squats
Corrects left-right imbalances
Strong glute and quad development
Trains balance and proprioception

description.en: The dumbbell squat is a compound lower-body exercise performed by holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides while squatting down and back up. It builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings without requiring a barbell or rack, making it ideal for home workouts and beginners. It is also a useful regression for anyone learning the squat pattern before progressing to the barbell.

en: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart and a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body.
Set your feet so toes point slightly outward. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Initiate the squat by sitting your hips back and down while bending your knees. Keep your chest tall.
Allow the dumbbells to hang straight down at your sides as you descend.
Squat down until your hip crease drops to or below the top of your knee (parallel or deeper).
Drive through your full foot to stand back up, squeezing your glutes at the top.
Keep your knees tracking in line with your toes throughout. Avoid letting them cave inward.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Increase load as form holds steady.
Builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings with minimal equipment
Excellent regression for learning squat mechanics before adding a barbell
Easy on the lower back compared to barbell back squats
Highly portable: can be done at home with a single pair of dumbbells
Trains grip and core stability through the loaded hold
Easy to scale up by increasing dumbbell weight or adding tempo and pauses

description.en: The dumbbell standing arms rotate trains external shoulder rotation with light dumbbells. With elbows tucked at your sides and arms bent to 90 degrees, you rotate the dumbbells outward by externally rotating the shoulders. The drill builds rotator cuff strength essential for shoulder health.

en: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
Bend your elbows to 90 degrees with forearms parallel to the floor.
Pin your elbows tightly against your sides.
Hold the dumbbells with palms facing each other.
Brace your core.
Rotate your forearms outward by externally rotating at the shoulders.
Continue until your forearms point out to the sides at 90 degrees.
Slowly rotate back to the starting position.
Builds rotator cuff strength
Improves shoulder health
Useful for rehab and prehab
Strict isolation of external rotators
Strong functional carryover
Easy to scale by changing dumbbell weight

description.en: The elbow arm circles are a shoulder mobility warm-up where the fingertips are placed on the shoulders and the elbows circle in a wide arc. The bent-arm circles open up the shoulders and warm up the rotator cuff for upper body training.

en: Stand tall with feet at hip-width.
Place your fingertips on top of each shoulder.
Keep the arms bent at the elbows.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Begin circling the elbows forward in big arcs.
Reach the elbows up high and bring them down low.
Continue several circles in one direction.
Reverse the direction and circle the elbows backward.
Mobilizes the shoulders
Warms up the rotator cuff
No equipment needed
Useful warm-up move
Easy to add to any session
Improves shoulder mobility

description.en: The finger push-up (fingertip push-up) performs push-ups with the hands supported on fingertips rather than flat palms. It builds extreme finger and hand strength alongside the standard push-up muscles. It is popular in martial arts training.

en: Get into a push-up position. Instead of flat palms, support yourself on your fingertips.
Spread fingers wide for stability. Arch your fingers like claws.
Perform push-ups from this fingertip position.
Lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up.
Maintain straight body line.
Start with fewer fingers (all five) and progress to fewer over time.
Begin with incline fingertip push-ups if full floor version is too hard.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps. Build up gradually to protect your fingers.
Builds extreme finger and hand strength
Popular in martial arts training
Develops grip strength from a unique angle
Advanced push-up variation
No equipment needed
Impressive demonstration of hand strength

description.en: The glute ham twist is a glute ham developer hold combined with torso rotation. The lifter sets up on the GHD with the body extended and rotates the upper body from side to side at the top. The twist loads the lower back rotators and obliques.

en: Set up on a glute ham developer with thighs on the pad.
Hook your feet in the pad supports.
Extend your body so it forms a straight line from head to heel.
Place your hands behind your head or across your chest.
Hold the extended position with the core braced.
Rotate the torso slowly to one side.
Return to center and rotate to the other side.
Continue alternating rotations with control.
Loads the lower back rotators
Strong oblique builder
Trains posterior chain
Strong GHD variation
Builds rotational strength
Useful core finisher

description.en: The Hyght dumbbell fly (developed by Chris Hyght) is a chest fly variation where you start with the dumbbells touching at the bottom and sweep them out and up in a wide arc. The unique path creates a longer, more active chest contraction than standard flys, with greater stimulus on the inner chest fibers.

en: Lie on a flat bench holding light dumbbells. Plant your feet flat. Brace your core.
Start with both dumbbells touching directly above your chest at lockout, palms facing each other.
From the top, lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc with a slight elbow bend.
Lower until you feel a deep chest stretch — typically when your arms are level with your shoulders.
Reverse the motion: sweep the dumbbells up and back together in a wide arc, focusing on squeezing your chest.
Bring the dumbbells back to touching at the top.
Squeeze your chest hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds.
Use lighter weight than standard flys. Form is everything.
Greater chest activation than standard flys
Targets the inner chest fibers
Longer time under tension
Builds chest size
Provides unique stimulus
Useful variation for plateau breaking

description.en: The jackknife is an advanced Pilates mat exercise where you lie on your back, roll your legs overhead toward the floor, then lift them straight up toward the ceiling, balancing on your shoulders before rolling back down. It demands extreme core control, hamstring flexibility, and shoulder strength. Avoid if you have neck issues.

en: Lie on your back with arms at your sides, legs extended straight up toward the ceiling.
Press your palms into the floor. Brace your core.
Exhale and use your core to lift your hips off the floor, rolling your legs overhead toward the floor behind your head (rollover).
Once your toes touch the floor (or as close as your flexibility allows), inhale.
Exhale and lift your legs straight up toward the ceiling, balancing on your shoulders.
Pause briefly with legs vertical and torso supported by your shoulders.
Slowly roll back down one vertebra at a time, lowering your legs back to vertical.
Repeat for 3 to 6 reps. Do not perform if you have neck or upper-back issues.
Builds extreme core control
Stretches the hamstrings and entire posterior chain
Develops shoulder and upper-back strength
Advanced Pilates exercise
Decompresses the spine
Trains controlled spinal articulation

description.en: The standing knee raise is a simple mobility and activation drill where you stand on one leg and drive the other knee up toward your chest, holding briefly before lowering. It activates the hip flexors, builds standing balance, and is one of the simplest hip-prep drills available.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms relaxed at your sides or extended forward for balance.
Stand on your left leg with a slight knee bend.
Drive your right knee up toward your chest as high as comfortable.
Use your hands to gently pull the knee closer if you can reach.
Hold for 1 to 2 seconds at the top.
Lower your right foot back to the floor.
Repeat with the left knee.
Continue alternating for 10 to 15 reps per side as a warm-up.
Activates the hip flexors
Builds standing balance
Excellent pre-workout warm-up
Improves hip mobility
No equipment needed
Quick and accessible

description.en: The lying floor hyperextension is a prone floor exercise where you lift your chest off the floor using your lower back muscles. It is essentially the same as the lower back curl and Superman — targeting the erector spinae with no equipment.

en: Lie face down. Hands behind your head or at your sides.
Legs on the floor.
Lift your chest and upper body off the floor by contracting your lower back.
Rise as high as comfortable.
Hold for 1 to 2 seconds. Squeeze your lower back.
Lower under control.
Move with control — no jerking.
Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Strengthens the erector spinae from the floor
No equipment needed
Builds lower back endurance
Beginner-friendly
Useful for back health
Accessible anywhere

description.en: The lying single leg reverse biceps curl with towel is a creative bodyweight curl. With a towel looped under one foot, the leg provides resistance against an overhand reverse grip curl.

en: Lie on your back with the legs extended.
Loop a towel under the arch of one foot.
Grip both ends of the towel with one hand using an overhand grip.
Lift the leg slightly off the floor for tension.
Brace the core and keep the upper arm fixed.
Curl the hand toward the shoulder by bending the elbow.
Squeeze the biceps and forearms at the top.
Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Builds biceps and forearm strength with bodyweight.
Reverse grip emphasizes the brachialis and brachioradialis.
No equipment needed beyond a towel.
Useful for travel or home training.
Trains one arm at a time for symmetry.
Easy to scale by adjusting leg tension.

description.en: The lever seated shoulder press is a vertical pressing exercise performed on a dedicated shoulder press machine with a guided path. The back support and fixed motion eliminate core and lower-back demand, allowing you to focus purely on pressing overhead. It is an excellent choice for beginners, for training to failure, or as heavy volume work after free-weight pressing.

en: Adjust the seat height so the handles are at roughly shoulder height when seated.
Sit with your back firmly against the pad. Grip the handles with an overhand grip.
Brace your core, pull your shoulders down and back, and plant your feet flat on the floor.
Press the handles straight up by extending at the elbows and shoulders. Exhale as you press.
Continue pressing until your arms are fully extended overhead (or nearly so). Do not hyperextend.
Lower the handles under control back to shoulder height over two seconds.
Stop just before the weight stack touches down to maintain tension on the shoulders.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Guided path and back support allow pure shoulder focus
Eliminates core and lower-back demand
Allows safe training to failure with no spotter needed
Easy to load progressively in small increments
Excellent for beginners learning the pressing pattern
Useful for high-volume shoulder training

description.en: The medicine ball around head rotation is a shoulder and core endurance drill. Circling a medicine ball around the head loads the delts isometrically while the core fights the shifting weight.

en: Stand tall with the feet shoulder width apart.
Hold a medicine ball with both hands at chest level.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Press the ball forward and circle it around the head.
Continue circling to one side around the back.
Bring the ball back to the front and continue.
Keep the arms slightly bent throughout.
Reverse direction at the halfway point.
Trains the shoulders.
Loads the core for stability.
Builds shoulder endurance.
Useful conditioning drill.
Improves coordination.

description.en: The medicine ball chest push from 3 point stance is a sport specific power drill that combines a football style start with a chest throw. The 3 point stance forces the lifter to drive up and forward at the same time as the chest push.

en: Set up in a 3 point stance holding a medicine ball at chest level with one hand.
Set the other hand on the floor in front for support.
Brace the core and keep the back flat.
Drive up and forward explosively.
Push the ball into the air or against a wall with both hands.
Land in an athletic stance.
Reset to the 3 point stance.
Continue for the working set.
Builds explosive power.
Trains acceleration.
Sport specific drill.
Useful for football and field sports.
Improves total body power.

description.en: The medicine ball chest push with run release is an athletic conditioning drill that combines a chest throw with a sprint. After throwing the ball forward, the lifter sprints to chase it down which trains explosive power and acceleration.

en: Stand on an open field or court holding a medicine ball at chest level.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Throw the ball forward as far as possible.
Drive off the back foot to begin the sprint.
Sprint hard to retrieve the ball.
Pick the ball up at full speed.
Decelerate and reset to the start.
Continue for the working set.
Builds explosive chest power.
Trains acceleration.
Brutal conditioning drill.
Useful for athletes.
Improves total body power.

description.en: The negative dragon flag performs only the lowering (eccentric) phase of the dragon flag. You lie on a bench, grip behind your head, raise your body to vertical, then slowly lower it to horizontal under control. The slow eccentric builds the core strength needed for full dragon flags.

en: Lie on a sturdy bench. Grip the bench behind your head.
Roll up to a vertical position — legs and body pointing to the ceiling, supported on your upper back.
Keeping your body straight (like a plank), slowly lower yourself toward horizontal.
Lower over 5 to 10 seconds. Control the descent.
Do not let your body bend at the hips — stay straight like a flag.
Once horizontal (or as low as you can control), reset to vertical and repeat.
This is extremely demanding. Start with 3 to 5 slow negatives.
Progress toward holding static positions and eventually full reps.
Builds toward full dragon flags
Eccentric training builds core strength effectively
Extremely demanding anti-extension exercise
Develops the straight-body control needed for dragon flags
Progressive — control longer lowering times
Advanced core progression

description.en: The pike to cobra push-up is a dynamic exercise where you start in a pike (downward dog) position, perform a push-up while sweeping your body forward into a cobra position, then push back into the pike. It builds shoulder strength, chest mobility, and full-body coordination — a yoga-inspired strength flow.

en: Start in a downward-facing dog pose — hips lifted high, body in an inverted V.
Bend your arms and lower your head toward the floor in a pike push-up motion.
As you lower, sweep your body forward and down — like a wave motion.
Continue until your hips are near the floor and your chest is lifted in a cobra position.
From cobra, push your hips up and back, returning to the downward dog pike position.
That is one rep.
Move smoothly with the breath. Keep your arms working throughout.
Aim for 5 to 10 reps with control.
Combines pike push-up strength with cobra mobility
Builds shoulder strength and chest flexibility
Develops body control and coordination
No equipment needed
Excellent dynamic warm-up
Trains shoulder mobility under load

description.en: The quickly trot in place is a cardio drill that runs in place at a fast tempo. The mover lifts the knees and pumps the arms to mimic running. It is a useful warm-up drill or low impact cardio finisher.

en: Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Bend the elbows at ninety degrees.
Begin lifting the knees up in a fast trot.
Land on the balls of the feet.
Pump the arms in opposition to the legs.
Maintain a fast tempo throughout.
Continue for the working set.
Burns calories
Strong warm-up drill
Trains the legs
Builds cardio capacity
Useful for conditioning
No equipment needed

description.en: The roll ball lateral vastus is a self myofascial release drill for the outer quad. Pressing a ball into the vastus lateralis releases knots that contribute to knee tracking issues and IT band tightness.

en: Lie on one side on the floor.
Place a massage ball under the outer thigh.
Stack the legs or stagger them for balance.
Brace the body on the bottom forearm.
Keep the upper body relaxed.
Roll the outer thigh slowly over the ball.
Pause on tender spots for several breaths.
Cover from hip to knee then switch sides.
Releases the outer quad.
Improves knee tracking.
Reduces IT band tightness.
Useful for runners.
Joint friendly release.

description.en: The run and semi squat jump alternates running in place with squat jumps. The lifter runs in place for several seconds, then drops into a half squat and explodes up into a jump. The combo trains cardio capacity and lower body power.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and start running in place.
Drive the knees up high with quick steps.
Run in place for several seconds.
Stop and drop into a half squat with thighs at half depth.
Drive through the heels to explode up into a jump.
Land softly and immediately start running in place again.
Continue alternating runs and squat jumps.
Brutal cardio combo
Trains explosive power
Builds cardio capacity
Strong functional pattern
Useful conditioning combo
Builds the glutes

description.en: The seated neck stretch is a series of gentle neck tilts performed from a seated position to relieve tension in the upper traps, levator scapulae, and sides of the neck. It is one of the most practical stretches for office workers and anyone who experiences neck tightness from screens.

en: Sit tall in a chair with feet flat on the floor. Pull your shoulders back and down.
Tilt your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder.
Place your right hand gently on the left side of your head and apply light pressure.
Keep your left shoulder pulled down — do not let it shrug toward your ear.
Hold for 20 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Release and repeat on the left side.
For variation: tilt forward (chin to chest), back (looking up), and rotate left/right.
Apply only gentle pressure. Never force the neck stretch.
Relieves neck and trap tension
Practical for office and desk settings
No equipment needed
Quick and easy — takes less than 2 minutes
Counteracts screen-time neck strain
Improves posture awareness

description.en: The side push neck stretch is an isometric neck strengthening move. The lifter places the hand against the side of the head and pushes while the neck resists. The static contraction builds neck strength and improves mobility.

en: Sit or stand tall with the chest open.
Place one hand against the side of the head above the ear.
Brace your core and keep the spine tall.
Push the hand into the head firmly.
Resist the push with the neck so the head stays still.
Hold the isometric contraction with steady breath.
Release the press slowly.
Switch sides and repeat.
Strong isometric neck builder
Builds neck strength
No equipment needed
Useful for athletes
Builds neck stability
Strong neck move

description.en: The single-leg box jump is an advanced plyometric exercise where you jump onto a box from one leg. It builds tremendous unilateral power, balance, and ankle stability. It demands perfect landing mechanics and should only be attempted after mastering two-leg box jumps.

en: Stand on one leg facing a box (start with a low box — 12 to 18 inches).
Slightly bend your standing knee. Swing your arms back to load the jump.
Explosively swing your arms forward and up while pushing off your standing leg.
Jump onto the box, landing on the same single leg you launched from.
Land softly with a bent knee to absorb the impact. Stick the landing.
Step down (do NOT jump down) — protecting your knees and ankles.
Reset and complete all reps on one leg before switching.
Use low reps (3 to 5 per side) — this is a maximal-effort exercise.
Builds elite unilateral explosive power
Develops single-leg balance and stability
Carries over to sprinting and jumping sports
Exposes left-right power imbalances
Trains the ankle and knee for landing forces
Impressive plyometric skill

description.en: The single leg glute bridge with knee to chest is a unilateral glute drill. Holding the off leg knee pulled tight to the chest while bridging on the other foot shifts the entire load onto the working glute.

en: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat.
Pull one knee tight to the chest with both hands.
Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes.
Brace the core and keep the chest up.
Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips.
Squeeze the working glute hard at the top.
Lower the hips with control to the start.
Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Isolates one glute.
Knee to chest fixes the off side.
Bodyweight move.
Useful for glute imbalances.
Builds glute strength.

description.en: Skips are a foundational athletic warm-up and cardio drill where you alternate hopping on each foot while driving the opposite knee up. They build calf elasticity, hip flexor power, coordination, and rhythm. They are a staple in track and field warm-ups and can be performed in place or moving forward.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Hop forward (or in place) on your right foot while driving your left knee up toward your chest.
Land back on your left foot as your right knee comes up.
Continue alternating in a skipping rhythm.
Pump your arms naturally in opposition to the legs.
Stay on the balls of your feet. Land softly.
Aim for both height and quick turnover.
Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set or for distance.
Builds calf elasticity and ankle stiffness
Develops hip flexor power
Improves coordination and rhythm
Excellent cardio warm-up
Foundational track and field drill
No equipment needed

description.en: The Smith one arm row is performed at a Smith machine with the bar set low. Standing perpendicular to the bar, you grip it with one hand and row it up to your hip. The fixed bar path eliminates balance demands while the single-arm pattern allows focused back work and corrects imbalances.

en: Set the Smith machine bar at hip height.
Stand perpendicular to the bar with your right side toward it.
Grip the bar with your right hand and step back into a bent over position.
Plant your left hand on a bench or your left thigh for support.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Row the bar up by driving your right elbow back toward your hip.
Squeeze your right shoulder blade at the top.
Lower the bar back down with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Single-arm back work corrects imbalances
Smith fixed bar path eliminates balance demands
Builds back size and thickness
Strong lat engagement
Useful for hypertrophy training
Allows progressive heavy loading

description.en: The standing forward bend Uttanasana is a foundational yoga forward fold. The mover hinges at the hips and folds the torso toward the legs while letting the head hang. It stretches the hamstrings and lengthens the spine.

en: Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Inhale and lift the chest.
Exhale and hinge at the hips folding forward.
Let the hands hang down toward the floor or shins.
Soften the knees if needed.
Let the head hang heavy.
Hold the pose then rise with a flat back.
Stretches the hamstrings
Lengthens the spine
Strong yoga pose
Useful warm-up
Builds posterior chain flexibility

description.en: The standing lateral stretch is a simple standing stretch where you reach one arm overhead and lean to the opposite side, opening the lats, obliques, and intercostals on the reaching side. It is one of the most accessible stretches for relieving side-body tightness from sitting and lifting.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
Reach your right arm straight up overhead.
Place your left hand on your left hip or let it hang.
Lean your torso to the left, reaching your right arm over to the left as you bend.
Keep both feet planted. Do not lean forward or backward.
Feel the deep stretch through your right side body — lat, obliques, and ribs.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply.
Return to standing. Switch sides and repeat.
Opens the lats, obliques, and intercostals
Improves lateral spinal flexibility
Counteracts hunched posture
Quick and accessible
No equipment needed
Excellent between-sets stretch

description.en: The suspender reverse fly uses suspension straps gripped above your head with the body angled below. By pulling the arms out to the sides in a fly motion, you train the rear delts and rhomboids. The strap setup makes the exercise easy to scale by changing your foot position.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor and grip the handles with both hands.
Walk your feet forward so your body angles back with arms extended.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Pull your hands out to the sides in a wide arc.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the back position.
Lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Bodyweight rear delt training
Easy to scale by changing foot position
Builds posterior shoulder strength
Improves posture
Useful for shoulder balance work
Excellent for home or travel training

description.en: The suspender side cross lunge uses TRX support during a lateral lunge where the working leg steps out and across the body. The cross-step works the adductors and glute medius while the strap helps balance through the side range.

en: Stand facing a suspension trainer with handles at chest height.
Hold the handles for light support.
Set your feet together and brace your core.
Step one foot out to the side and across the body.
Lower into a side cross lunge with the working knee bent.
Keep the trail leg straight with toes pointing forward.
Drive through the working leg heel to push back to standing.
Alternate legs each rep.
Trains adductors and glutes
Hits the glute medius
TRX support helps balance
Builds lateral strength
Useful for athletes
Strong unilateral leg move

description.en: The suspension trainer biceps clutch is a bodyweight bicep curl performed on TRX straps. The lifter grips the handles with palms up and curls the body up toward the hands by bending the elbows. The strap angle determines the difficulty. It is a strong arm builder.

en: Set a suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with palms facing up.
Lean back so the body is at an angle with arms extended.
Brace your core and squeeze the glutes.
Bend the elbows to curl the body up toward the hands.
Keep the upper arms locked in place.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower with control to the start.
Bodyweight bicep curl
No dumbbells needed
Trains the biceps
Strong functional curl
Useful arm builder
Easy to scale by angle

description.en: The tiger tail hamstring roll is a self-myofascial release move using a stick massager. The lifter sits down and rolls the tool along the hamstrings to release tight tissue and knots. It is a useful warm-up and recovery move for tight hamstrings.

en: Sit down on the floor or a bench with one leg extended.
Hold the tiger tail stick by the handles with both hands.
Place the roller across the hamstring near the knee.
Press down with moderate pressure into the muscle.
Roll the stick up the hamstring toward the glute.
Pause on any tender spots to release the tissue.
Roll back down to the knee and repeat the pass.
Continue rolling the full hamstring. Switch legs and repeat.
Releases tight hamstrings
Useful warm-up move
Speeds recovery
Easy to do anywhere
Trains tissue quality
No floor work needed

description.en: The weighted seated reverse wrist curl is a reverse wrist curl using dumbbells. The lifter sits with forearms resting on the thighs and dumbbells held with palms facing down, then curls the wrists up. The reverse grip targets the wrist extensors on top of the forearm.

en: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with a pronated overhand grip.
Rest the forearms on the thighs.
Let the wrists hang off the knees.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Set the dumbbells with palms facing down.
Curl the wrists up squeezing the top of the forearms.
Lift as high as the wrists allow.
Lower the wrists back down with control.
Strong wrist extensor builder
Trains the top forearms
Builds grip strength
Easy to scale loading
Useful arm builder
Strong dumbbell move

description.en: The wide to narrow push-up alternates hand position between wide (chest emphasis) and narrow (tricep emphasis) on each rep. It provides both stimuli in one continuous set.

en: Start in a wide push-up position. Perform one push-up.
Walk your hands inward to a narrow (close-grip) position.
Perform one push-up.
Walk your hands back out to wide. Push-up.
Continue alternating wide and narrow.
Maintain body alignment throughout the transitions.
Wide position emphasizes chest; narrow emphasizes triceps.
Aim for 8 to 12 total reps (4-6 per width).
Targets both chest and triceps in one set
Provides varied stimulus without rest
No equipment needed
Engaging push-up variation
Builds both pressing patterns
Time-efficient
